title: 1 Samuel 1:19–28
context: The LORD remembers Hannah, and she bears Samuel. After weaning him, she brings him with offerings to the LORD’s house in Shiloh and gives him to the LORD for as long as he lives.

verses.text: They rose up in the morning early and worshiped the LORD, then returned and came to their house to Ramah. Then Elkanah knew Hannah his wife; and the LORD remembered her.
verses.arminianNotes: The family worships, returns to Ramah, and “the LORD remembered her.” Arminian readers see God answering a prayer freely offered, responding to Hannah’s plea in her vow.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s remembering as his gracious action toward Hannah. Readers in both traditions commonly note that “remembered” signals God acting on behalf of his people, not that he had forgotten.

verses.text: When the time had come, Hannah conceived, and bore a son; and she named him Samuel, saying, “Because I have asked him of the LORD.”
verses.arminianNotes: Hannah bears a son and names him Samuel, saying, “Because I have asked him of the LORD.” Arminian readers see a name that preserves the memory of prayer answered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the child’s name testifying to God as the giver. Samuel sounds like the Hebrew for “heard by God,” linking the name to answered prayer.

verses.text: The man Elkanah, and all his house, went up to offer to the LORD the yearly sacrifice and his vow.
verses.arminianNotes: Elkanah and his household go up to offer the yearly sacrifice and his vow. Arminian readers see the family continuing faithful worship and Elkanah honoring his own vow.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see regular worship continuing after the answer to prayer. Gratitude is expressed through the ordinary rhythms of sacrifice that God had appointed for Israel.

verses.text: But Hannah didn’t go up, for she said to her husband, “Not until the child is weaned; then I will bring him, that he may appear before the LORD, and stay there forever.”
verses.arminianNotes: Hannah tells her husband, “Not until the child is weaned; then I will bring him.” Arminian readers see her planning faithfully to fulfill her vow at the right time.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Hannah’s intention to keep her promise in full. Her phrase “stay there forever” shows that her dedication of Samuel is wholehearted and permanent.

verses.text: Elkanah her husband said to her, “Do what seems good to you. Wait until you have weaned him; only may the LORD establish his word.” So the woman waited and nursed her son until she weaned him.
verses.arminianNotes: Elkanah says, “Do what seems good to you … only may the LORD establish his word.” Arminian readers see a husband supporting his wife’s vow and entrusting the outcome to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the prayer that the LORD would establish his word as reliance on God to bring his purposes to completion. The WEB prints “his word” here and does not mark a variant.

verses.text: When she had weaned him, she took him up with her, with three bulls, and one ephah of meal, and a container of wine, and brought him to the LORD’s house in Shiloh. The child was young.
verses.arminianNotes: After weaning, Hannah brings Samuel to Shiloh with three bulls, an ephah of meal, and wine. Arminian readers see a generous offering that accompanies her costly gift of her son.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see thankful worship accompanying the dedication. The ephah is explained here only as a dry measure; the edition reads “three bulls” without a textual note.

verses.text: They killed the bull, and brought the child to Eli.
verses.arminianNotes: They kill the bull and bring the child to Eli. Arminian readers see the sacrifice and the presentation of Samuel joined, showing that the dedication is an act of worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Samuel brought into the LORD’s service through worship at the sanctuary. The child is entrusted to the very priest whose house will soon face judgment.

verses.text: She said, “Oh, my lord, as your soul lives, my lord, I am the woman who stood by you here, praying to the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Hannah says, “Oh, my lord, as your soul lives, my lord, I am the woman who stood by you here, praying to the LORD.” Arminian readers see her testimony linking past prayer and present answer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Hannah publicly recalling God’s answer. Her words remind Eli of the earlier scene and invite him to recognize what God has done.

verses.text: I prayed for this child, and the LORD has given me my petition which I asked of him.
verses.arminianNotes: She says, “I prayed for this child, and the LORD has given me my petition which I asked of him.” Arminian readers see grateful testimony to God’s gracious response to prayer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God honored as the giver of the child. Readers in both traditions commonly see this verse as encouragement to bring requests to God and to give thanks openly when he answers.

verses.text: Therefore I have also given him to the LORD. As long as he lives he is given to the LORD.” He worshiped the LORD there.
verses.arminianNotes: Hannah says, “Therefore I have also given him to the LORD,” and worship follows. Arminian readers see her free fulfillment of her vow, returning God’s gift to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a mother giving back what God gave, recognizing that the child belongs to him. The chapter closes in worship, preparing for Hannah’s song.
